clinicalPearls: Defined electrophysiologically by preserved outer hair cell function (present otoacoustic emissions and/or cochlear microphonic) with an absent or grossly abnormal auditory brainstem response
Speech discrimination is often disproportionately poor relative to the pure-tone audiogram, and hearing may appear to fluctuate
Risk factors include prematurity, hyperbilirubinaemia, hypoxia, and neonatal intensive care, alongside genetic causes such as OTOF variants
Behavioural thresholds can range from near-normal to profound, so the audiogram alone underestimates the functional deficit
Standard newborn screening using otoacoustic emissions alone will miss ANSD, so automated brainstem response screening is needed in at-risk infants
Amplification benefit is variable and unpredictable, whereas cochlear implantation is often effective, particularly with a synaptopathic (presynaptic) lesion
Distinguishing a presynaptic cochlear synaptopathy from a true neural (nerve) lesion guides prognosis and implant candidacy
reference.pathophysiology: In auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder the cochlear outer hair cells continue to function, so otoacoustic emissions and the cochlear microphonic persist, but transmission of a synchronised signal along the auditory pathway is disrupted. The lesion may be presynaptic, at the inner hair cell to auditory nerve synapse (synaptopathy, as with otoferlin dysfunction), or neural, affecting spiral ganglion neurones or the auditory nerve itself. Loss of neural synchrony degrades the timing cues that underpin speech understanding, especially in noise, which explains why discrimination is far worse than the pure-tone thresholds would predict. The distinction between synaptopathic and neural forms is central because a functioning nerve can be stimulated directly by a cochlear implant.
additionalDifferentials: Otoferlin-related deafness (DFNB9) as a specific synaptopathic cause
Cochlear sensorineural loss with absent emissions from outer hair cell damage
Retrocochlear pathology such as vestibular schwannoma or demyelination
Charcot-Marie-Tooth and other peripheral neuropathies with auditory involvement
additionalInvestigations: Auditory brainstem response demonstrating absent or dyssynchronous waveforms
Otoacoustic emissions and dedicated cochlear microphonic recording with stimulus polarity reversal
Behavioural audiometry and speech perception testing appropriate to age
Genetic testing including OTOF and broader deafness and neuropathy panels
Cross-sectional imaging to assess the cochlear nerve and exclude retrocochlear lesions
Assessment for associated peripheral neuropathy where clinically suggested
redFlags: Speech understanding far worse than the audiogram implies, with resulting language delay
Missed diagnosis in an at-risk neonate screened by emissions alone
Signs of a wider peripheral neuropathy or a retrocochlear mass
Progressive deterioration suggesting an evolving neural process
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely; some children with milder or maturational forms improve, whereas persistent cases, especially synaptopathic ones, often do well with cochlear implantation, while true neural lesions carry a more guarded prognosis.
pitfalls: Relying on otoacoustic-emission-only newborn screening and missing the diagnosis
Interpreting present emissions as normal hearing without brainstem response testing
Failing to reverse stimulus polarity, mistaking a cochlear microphonic for a genuine neural response
Assuming hearing aids will suffice without evaluating implant candidacy in poor discriminators
